# Strict support improvement with one full tetrahedral row and two surviving zero rows

This note eliminates one particular regular maximizing stratum of the d=3 stochastic capacity problem. It is not a proof of the general stochastic theorem or of OC. The argument retains an actual tetrahedral section, forces two equal low vertex heights, and then constructs a strictly better zero-diagonal support value.

## 1. Definitions and statement

Let Delta={xi in R^4: xi_j>=0, sum xi_j=1}, with uniform probability measure. For x>=0 define

    F_x(t)=Pr(x dot Xi<=t),
    phi(x)=inf_{t>0,F_x(t)>0} t/F_x(t)^(1/3).

Let D_3 be the downward set of vectors dominated by the four off-diagonal row geometric means of nonnegative zero-diagonal column-stochastic 4 by 4 matrices. Its support function at c>=0 is h_3(c).

Consider H_c(X)=sum_i c_i phi(X_i), c_i>0, on all column-stochastic 4 by 4 matrices. Suppose a global maximizer has exactly one fully positive row r. Assume the capacity of this row is differentiable and its minimizing threshold is unique, proper, and regular: F_x(t) is jointly C^1 in x,t near the cut, with the usual coarea derivative formulas. After merging proportional rows with the same unique zero column, suppose exactly two nonzero one-zero rows remain and one row s is identically zero. Then this situation is impossible: there is a zero-diagonal matrix whose weighted geometric-mean objective strictly exceeds H_c(X).

The theorem allows a putative regular threshold through a vertex; the proof excludes that incidence rather than discarding it by assumption. Merging is legitimate because the maximizing first-order equations force rows with the same missing column to have equal weights and proportional entries. No assertion is made here about maxima with multiple full rows or nonregular capacity minima.

## 2. Actual maximizing equations

Here we record, with their derivations, the needed equations from `candidate 6a014eb26413a72b`. Permute columns so that the two surviving one-zero rows have their zeros on their diagonals. The unmatched column labels are r and s. Write x for the full row, t for its minimizing threshold, F=F_x(t), and b for the actual barycentric centroid of the section x dot xi=t.

At an interior minimizing threshold, tF'=3F. Coarea gives partial_j F=-F'b_j. Differentiating the touching fixed-threshold ratio therefore gives partial_j phi=F^(-1/3)b_j. Column-preserving transfers with the full row give positive column multipliers lambda_j.

A row i with its unique zero at i has capacity equal to the geometric mean of its other entries. For mu_i=c_i phi(X_i)/3, the positive-entry equations are

    X_ij=mu_i/lambda_j (j!=i),
    c_i=3 GM(lambda_except_i).

The one-sided derivative on introducing a missing entry is GM(z)[1/min z-(sum 1/z)/3]. Thus maximality gives 3 max_{j!=i}lambda_j<=sum lambda_j. Two distinct missing columns imply 3lambda_j<=sum lambda for every j. The derivative formula is valid also for repeated positive entries: in the perturbed row the minimizing threshold tends to min z, and the full-orthant lower cap bound and the ratio at min z squeeze its first derivative to the displayed expression.

Normalize the multipliers, and all objective weights, so that sum lambda=1. Euler homogeneity and the column sums then give H_c(X)=1. The full-row gradient gives lambda=b and c_r=F^(1/3). Consequently

    b_j>0, sum b_j=1, b_j<=1/3,
    c_i=3 GM(b_except_i) for i not in {r,s},
    c_r=F^(1/3), H_c(X)=1.                              (1)

Set mu_r=mu_s=0, and mu=sum mu_i. Column stochasticity gives

    b_j(1-x_j)=mu-mu_j, mu=(1-t)/3.                    (2)

Indeed summing the first equations gives 1-t=3mu. Both surviving zero rows have positive off-diagonal entries, so every column has a positive entry outside the full row. Thus 0<x_j<1 for all j. Define

    q_j=(1-x_j)b_j/(1-t).

Then q_r=q_s=1/3 and the other two q_j are strictly less than 1/3. In particular (2), b_r,b_s<=1/3 imply x_r,x_s<=t.

There must be at least two strictly captured vertices. To justify this additional geometric restriction, let F_j be the fraction captured in the opposite facet xi_j=0. The tangent affine vector field e_j-xi has divergence -3. The divergence theorem on the cut tetrahedron gives

    3F_j=3F+(x_j-t)F'.

Thus stationarity gives F_j=(x_j/t)F>0 for every j. If only one vertex were strictly captured, its opposite facet would have zero captured area, a contradiction. This argument also covers cuts through vertices and edges; their lower-dimensional boundaries do not affect the facet areas.

## 3. The transformed section has exactly two captured vertices

On the actual section apply the positive diagonal linear map

    Z_j=(1-x_j)xi_j/(1-t).

The image lies in Delta and is the section

    sum_j a_j Z_j=1/3, a_j=(1-t)/[3(1-x_j)].           (3)

The map is invertible and has one constant area Jacobian on the section plane. Hence uniform section measure maps to uniform section measure; its centroid is exactly q. At the unmatched labels, (2) gives a_r=b_r and a_s=b_s. Moreover a_j-1/3 and x_j-t have the same sign, so all vertex incidences are preserved.

Neither r nor s can lie on the cut. If both did, properness would leave at most one strictly captured vertex, already impossible. If only r did, the preceding facet-positivity argument requires two strictly captured vertices among the other three. The fourth vertex is then excluded, and the section is a triangle bounding a vertex cap at that excluded vertex. A strictly captured vertex s contributes to its section centroid only through its incident edge intercept, which is strictly less than one. Therefore q_s<1/3, contradiction. Additional boundary vertices leave too few strictly captured vertices and have already been excluded.

Thus r,s are strictly captured. If either other vertex were also weakly captured, properness leaves one excluded vertex and the section is again the triangle bounding its vertex cap, including a possible edge intercept equal to one. Since r is strictly captured, q_r<1/3, again impossible. Therefore precisely r,s are strictly captured and the other two vertices are strictly excluded. The section is quadrilateral.

Parameterize its captured vertex heights relative to its cut by -1/X,-1/Y and its excluded heights by 1/Z,1/W, with X,Y,Z,W>0 and T=X+Y+Z+W. The quadrilateral centroid is

    3q_r=X[1/(X+Z)+1/(X+W)-1/T],
    3q_s=Y[1/(Y+Z)+1/(Y+W)-1/T].

For completeness, its four vertices are the intersections on the four captured-to-excluded edges. Their two diagonals meet at (X,Y,Z,W)/T. Triangulating along either diagonal gives the centroid equal to one third of the sum of the four vertices minus their diagonal intersection, yielding these formulas.

The equations q_r=q_s=1/3 become

    ZW(T+X)=YX^2, ZW(T+Y)=XY^2.

Multiplying the first by Y, the second by X, and subtracting gives ZWT(Y-X)=0. Hence X=Y. The captured distances to the transformed cutting plane are equal, so a_r=a_s and then

    b_r=b_s=:A<1/3, x_r=x_s=:alpha<t.                 (4)

This is an incidence and first-moment consequence, not a symmetry assumption on the original matrix.

## 4. Exact section and cap formulas

Let beta,gamma be the two excluded full-row entries. Put

    p=(t-alpha)/(beta-alpha), q=(t-alpha)/(gamma-alpha),
    u=1-p, v=1-q, S=u+v, P=uv, rho=P/S^2.

Here 0<u,v<1 and 0<rho<=1/4. Denote the section-centroid coordinates at beta,gamma by C,D. Then

    A=(u^2+uv+v^2)/(3S)=S(1-rho)/3,
    C=(1-u)(2u+v)/(3S), D=(1-v)(u+2v)/(3S),
    F=(1-u)(1-v)(1+S).                               (5)

These formulas follow directly by integrating actual tetrahedral measure. Its marginal density on the two excluded barycentric coordinates z,w is 6(1-z-w). The captured region is the triangle z/p+w/q<=1. Integrating gives F=pq(3-p-q). On the section line z=p tau,w=q(1-tau), the coarea weight is proportional to l(tau)=v+(u-v)tau. Its integral is S/2. The means of z,w are the displayed C,D. Conditional on z,w the two low coordinates are uniform on their interval with sum l; each has mean l/2. Thus their section mean is (1/2) integral l^2/integral l=(u^2+uv+v^2)/(3S).

Write V=(1-u)(1-v). Useful consequences are

    C+D=1-2A,
    CD=V(2+rho)/9,
    C-D=(u-v)(1-2S)/(3S).                             (6)

The constraints C,D<=1/3 are respectively u+S>=1 and v+S>=1. Summing gives S>=2/3. Equation (4) gives

    2/3<=S<1/(1-rho)<=4/3.                           (7)

## 5. A tetrahedral cap product used below

For any quadrilateral tetrahedral cap capturing vertices 0,1, if its section-centroid coordinate at 1 is at most 1/3, then its volume fraction satisfies

    F>27 b_1 b_2 b_3.                                (8)

Here is the exact algebraic certificate proved in `candidate 3ed628996d1cbb09`. Use positive diagonal parameters X,Y,Z,W as in Section 3, T their sum, R=Z+W, and B0=ZW. The hypothesis is precisely c=B0(T+Y)-XY^2>=0. Put

    B=R(X+Y)+X^2+XY+Y^2,
    E=R^3+2R^2X+3R^2Y+RX^2+5RXY+3RY^2
                                     +2X^2Y+2XY^2+Y^3.

The actual cap fraction equals

    B0[(X+Y)T-XY+B0]/[(X+Z)(X+W)(Y+Z)(Y+W)].

Substitution of the actual section-centroid formulas gives the polynomial identity

    F-27 b_1 b_2 b_3
      =B0[cB+B0 E+B0^2Y]/[T^3(Y+Z)^2(Y+W)^2]>0.

Every denominator is positive and B0 E>0. This proves (8) with no unproved inequality. In our case it yields F>27 ACD.

## 6. Exact support on the three-coordinate face

The coordinate-face identity from `candidate df39f37487bbac05` specializes to

    h_3(c_0,c_1,c_2,0)
       =h_2(c_0^(3/2),c_1^(3/2),c_2^(3/2))^(2/3).   (9)

A direct proof is short. Move any inactive-row column mass to an active row, avoiding its diagonal; this only increases the objective. The three active columns then form a zero-diagonal column-stochastic 3 by 3 matrix, whose row geometric means are g_i. If theta_i are the allocations in the fourth column, the objective is sum c_i g_i^(2/3)theta_i^(1/3). Holder, with equality at theta_i proportional to c_i^(3/2)g_i, makes its maximum (sum c_i^(3/2)g_i)^(2/3). Maximizing over the three-column matrix proves (9), including zero cases.

In (1),(4), put G=27A^2. Dropping the positive weight on the identically zero row gives the transformed three weights

    W=(sqrt F,sqrt(GD),sqrt(GC)).

For arbitrary positive W define eta_i=W_jW_k/(2W_i), and H=sum eta_i. If eta_i<=H/2 for all i, the exact support is h_2(W)=H. Indeed W_i=2sqrt(eta_j eta_k), and weighted AM-GM bounds the objective by sum eta. Equality is attained by the actual zero-diagonal column-stochastic matrix

    Z_ij=(H/2-eta_i)/eta_j for i!=j.

Its column sums equal one. Its row contribution is H-2eta_i, whose sum is H. Thus there is no unattained duality assertion here.

For our W, the three required triangle inequalities on eta are exactly

    GCD<=F(C+D), F|C-D|<=GCD.                         (10)

The first is strict: (8) gives F>27ACD, while C+D=1-2A>A, so F(C+D)>27A^2CD.

For the second, substitute (5)--(6), cancel the positive V/3, and use S>=2/3. The result is

    (1+S)(2S-1)sqrt(1-4rho)
       <=S^2(1-rho)^2(2+rho).

The function (1+S)(2S-1)/S^2=2+1/S-1/S^2 is increasing for 0<S<2. By (7), it suffices that

    (2+rho-rho^2)sqrt(1-4rho)<=(1-rho)^2(2+rho).

Both sides are nonnegative. Their squared difference is

    rho^2[rho^4+4rho^3-15rho^2-6rho+28]>0,

since the bracket is at least 28-15/16-6/4=409/16 on 0<rho<=1/4. This proves (10), including rho=1/4, where the left side of the unsquared inequality vanishes.

## 7. Strict payment by a positive polynomial certificate

The exact active support now is

    H=[F(C+D)+GCD]/[2sqrt(FCD)]
     =[3+(1+2rho)S-rho(1-rho^2)S^2]
                                      /[2sqrt((1+S)(2+rho))]. (11)

Let N be the numerator in the second expression and z=1-(1-rho)S. By (7), 0<z<1. The exact Bernstein identity is

    (1-rho)^2[N^2-4(1+S)(2+rho)]
      =sum_{i=0}^4 binom(4,i) B_i z^i(1-z)^(4-i),    (12)

where

    B_0=rho^4,
    B_1=rho^2(7-4rho)/2,
    B_2=[(1-4rho)^2+18rho^2(1-rho)]/6,
    B_3=(1-rho)(1-2rho)(1-4rho)/2,
    B_4=(1-rho)^2(1-4rho).

All coefficients are nonnegative for 0<rho<=1/4; B_0>0 and 1-z>0 make the entire expression strictly positive. N is positive because (11) is the sum of the positive eta_i. Therefore H>1.

Equations (9)--(12) show

    h_3(c)>=h_3(c with coordinate s set to zero)=H^(2/3)>1=H_c(X).

The support maximum is attained by a zero-diagonal column-stochastic matrix: use Z above and the explicit equality fourth-column allocation in Section 6. On a zero-diagonal row its capacity equals its off-diagonal geometric mean. This is an actual feasible competitor with larger weighted capacity, contradicting global maximality. The theorem follows.

## 8. Scope and dependencies

This eliminates the regular one-full-row stratum with two surviving distinct positive one-zero rows. A single surviving row is already paid by the all-dimensional two-variable capacity theorem. Three distinct surviving one-zero rows are paid by the explicit central-section support matrix in `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`, Section 3. Thus all merged one-full-row cases with a unique proper regular differentiable full-row capacity minimum are now paid or excluded in d=3.

The argument does not treat two or more full rows, nonregular full-row capacity minima, or an arbitrary finite measure in place of uniform tetrahedral volume. It does not invoke the false general probability-only cubic statement. The cap product in Section 5 is stronger than the archived ordinary central-simplex depth theorem; the latter is not used here.

The companion exact verifier reconstructs (5)--(12), the actual section integrals, the diagonal equality equations, and rational feasible support matrices. Its finite checks supplement the complete algebraic proof, rather than establish a missing global theorem.
